doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: How the Beeches gigs taught him to play any style from the radio
summary: Caramanica explains that varied radio formats in the sixties forced musicians to play any style authentically, and advises students to diversify.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: On that gig at The Beeches. And I might as well ask you about that now, and I want to go back even further, but I thought when I got out of Fredonia after four years that I knew a lot about music. But then I started playing that gig and I found that I didn’t really know anything about playing a gig. And you and Rick Montalbano seemed to know all that stuff. And I’m curious as to why did you know the tunes to play and what worked in that situation? Where did that knowledge come from?
How did we know what tunes to play?
Well how did you know how to handle that particular gig, which was just a restaurant and people would dance. But where did you learn to do that?

Well you know I think that’s a good question. Historically if you look at what was happening in the sixties, it wasn’t so much — we had a radio station format that was all metal, it was all classic rock, it was all jazz, it was all country, it was all whatever. There were so many different kinds of music out there that appealed to so many different kinds of people, if you wanted to play a gig you had to know how to play a country tune with an authentic country feel, or a polka or, you know, any kind of thing. And of course we were in jazz so you had to listen to jazz. Well if you study enough of that kind of music, and I don’t mean like formally study but just like learn tunes and check them out, and you develop your ear, you have the ability to play just about anything that sounded authentic. So a new tune comes along and you say okay well that’s a little of this and a little of that, © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-

and I can do it. So you’re not just stuck with I can only play this style or that style. So I think that’s kind of what we had going for us. If you wanted to work, you had to be able to play whatever’s on the radio, and it could be any style.

Yes. And the radio, I remember recently looking at Billboard’s Top 10 from back in those years, and it was so varied. You could go from an Elvis song number one, and number two might be Mitch Miller. I mean, and the same playlist.

Right. And Sinatra with Basie. Yeah. All that Top 40 or whatever, it was very diversified. That changed a lot. And I think you mentioned in some of the pre-questions you gave me of things to think about, what to tell younger students who are interested in becoming musicians. And I want to skip to that because it goes right along with what we’re talking about is diversification of styles, learning more about not only how to play your instrument but, as much as I love jazz, there are other elements of music that make up that whole genre of jazz. And we’ve got the blues and we’ve got ballads and we’ve got big band stuff, and you’ve got chord and melody things in terms of the guitar, and the kids don’t study this. They say “I like Avenged Seven” I’m going to use these kinds of styles and sounds. And then when the music changes, as it will, it evolves, some other style comes in and they’re not aware of how to do that. You say if you want to be good at what you’re doing, diversify.
Okay. So you listened to the radio at that time, and you picked out tunes that you liked, or tunes that you may not have liked and you played them anyway.
